# The Book of Job — KJV, eBible eng-kjv2006 digital witness

## Bibliographic identity

The selected primary textual witness is the complete *Book of Job* in eBible.org's King James (Authorized) Version dataset `eng-kjv2006`. The acquired PDF contains 90 pages: Job 1:1–42:17 occupies PDF pages 1–89, labelled i–lxxxix; page 90, labelled xc, contains the edition and rights colophon. The colophon identifies a rendering made with Haiola and XeLaTeX on **19 August 2026**, from source files dated the same day. PDF metadata records creation at `D:20260819122458-10'00'`, creator LaTeX with hyperref, producer xdvipdfmx (20250410). The acquired bytes, rather than a mutable URL alone, identify this witness.

The colophon and [provider metadata](https://ebible.org/eng-kjv2006/copyright.htm) describe the standardized **1769** KJV text, protocanon, with Strong's numbers added in the edition dataset. This house identifies the actual Job PDF, including its verse numbering and footnotes; it does not infer that every dataset feature is printed in this file. `eng-kjv2006` is the provider's edition identifier. **2026 is the digital rendering date**, not Job's composition date or the date of the KJV translation. This is neither an original 1611 printed copy nor a diplomatic transcription of such a copy. No ancient author or date of composition is established by this acquisition. `Anonymous` is the author filing; KJV translation and eBible/Crosswire provision are separate bibliographic roles.

**Acquisition:** complete raw PDF: `working/sources-texts-references/biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006/eng-kjv2006_JOB.pdf`, downloaded from the selected URL on 8 September 2026, 361,689 bytes, SHA-256 `ed6ecb6c2670b33213d2a2227d38f330222ba9e2cda2ec7a1796af8794ce6ee6`. The PDF is the sole raw shelf copy. It contains no project commentary and is not a parallel passage house. All selected evidence, provenance and use boundaries live here.

**Rights:** the provider designates the text public domain and permits copying, while expressly recording a qualification for printing the translation in, or importing printed copies into, the United Kingdom. That notice is preserved in the raw colophon and linked metadata. The local research copy is recorded under that provider notice; this house does not assert unrestricted worldwide print-publication rights or undertake print distribution.

**Read scope:** all 42 chapters, all 1,070 numbered verses, all 89 text pages and the colophon were read from the acquired PDF in nine consecutive, untruncated ten-page batches. Text was extracted from the digital PDF with `pypdf`, not inferred from summaries or unchecked OCR. A separate verse-label check recovered 42 sequences, each beginning at 1 and increasing without a gap. Selected short quotations below were additionally checked against eBible's HTML rendering of the same `eng-kjv2006` edition. This HTML check is a second presentation of the same edition, not an independent textual tradition or a second selected translation.

## Source scholarship — the complete sequence

The following is **Paraphrased** from this witness. It records the book's narrative and speech sequence without imposing the later Mytheme's QL appointments. Speaker claims remain speaker claims, including when a speaker quotes or characterises another.

**Job 1:1–22 — household, first council and successive losses.** Job is introduced in Uz as upright, God-fearing and prosperous, with seven sons and three daughters. He sacrifices on his children's behalf after their feasts. In the council, the sons of God present themselves before the LORD and Satan appears among them. The LORD names Job's integrity; Satan challenges the disinterestedness of his reverence, pointing to his protection and prosperity. Permission to strike his possessions expressly excludes his person. Reports then follow one another: Sabean and Chaldean attacks, the destructive fire reported by a messenger, and the wind that kills his children. Job mourns and worships. The narrator affirms that he has not sinned or charged God foolishly. This evaluation belongs before the subsequent disputes.

**Job 2:1–13 — second council, the body, the wife and the first silence.** The council recurs, and the LORD affirms Job's continuing integrity while acknowledging the attack without cause. Satan now challenges integrity under bodily suffering; permission preserves Job's life. Job is afflicted with boils, scrapes himself with a potsherd and sits among ashes. His wife challenges his continuing integrity and urges him to curse God and die. He answers her by asking about receiving evil as well as good; the narrator qualifies the immediate response as sinless in his lips. His wife is unnamed in this text and reappears in Job's account of estrangement at 19:17. Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite come to mourn and comfort. They weep, rend their garments and sit with him for seven days and nights without speaking. Their first act must remain distinguishable from their later explanations.

**Job 3:1–26 — Job opens the discourse.** Job curses the day of his birth, wishes he had died before entering this life, and asks why the miserable are given light. He imagines death as relief shared by rulers, captives, masters and servants. He curses his day here; the text does not say that he has simply performed Satan's predicted curse against God.

**Job 4:1–5:27 — Eliphaz's first answer.** Eliphaz contrasts Job's earlier ability to strengthen others with his present distress. He invokes the destruction of evildoers and a nocturnal encounter questioning mortal purity before the maker. He urges Job to seek God, receive chastening and expect restoration. The vision and this counsel are Eliphaz's speech; their inclusion is not a narrator's endorsement of his diagnosis.

**Job 6:1–7:21 — the weight of grief and the demand to be heard.** Job asks that his calamity be weighed, describes divine arrows and the limits of his bodily strength, and longs for death. Friends should show pity; his companions have disappointed him like seasonal streams that fail those who rely on them. He invites genuine correction while challenging their attack on desperate speech. His address becomes a complaint to God about sleeplessness, bodily decay, relentless scrutiny and life's brevity.

**Job 8:1–22 — Bildad's appeal to inherited justice.** Bildad questions whether God could pervert judgement, invokes the children's transgression, and tells Job that uprightness would bring renewed prosperity. He appeals to ancestral teaching and images of a plant or fragile house whose apparent stability fails. His explanation of suffering must retain its speaker and its pressure upon a bereaved listener.

**Job 9:1–10:22 — the inaccessible judge and the made body.** Job acknowledges divine power while asking how a human being can contend with such a judge. He describes the lack of a daysman able to stand between them, the fear that prevents free speech, and the destruction of innocent and wicked alike. He asks why the hands that formed him from clay, clothed him with flesh and preserved his life should now destroy him. Divine making and destructive suffering remain together in the complaint.

**Job 11:1–20 — Zophar's first answer.** Zophar wishes God would speak against Job and reveal the wisdom Job lacks. He says Job's punishment is less than his iniquity merits and promises security after the removal of wickedness. His claim about Job's guilt is distinct from the prologue's account.

**Job 12:1–14:22 — disputed wisdom, address and mortality.** Job refuses the friends' monopoly on understanding. Beasts, earth and sea witness divine power, while social power and apparent wisdom can be overturned. He accuses the friends of deceitful advocacy for God and seeks an answer from God directly. This KJV witness retains trust and the defence of his own ways together at 13:15. The frailty of a human life and the possibility of a tree's renewal sharpen his question about death, remembrance and a future call to which he could answer. A single verse must not erase the surrounding complaint or settle other translations' textual questions.

**Job 15:1–17:16 — Eliphaz again, then Job.** Eliphaz treats Job's speech as self-condemnation, appeals to age and tradition, and elaborates the terror awaiting the wicked. Job calls the friends miserable comforters and imagines how he would strengthen them if their positions were exchanged. Neither speech nor silence presently relieves him. He describes being made a target and seeks a witness on high, while returning to bodily wasting, mockery and the grave.

**Job 18:1–19:29 — Bildad again, then Job.** Bildad describes the wicked caught in nets, darkness and terror, with family and remembrance extinguished. Job answers that words themselves are breaking him. He names estrangement from kin, servants, wife and intimates, asks for pity, and wishes his words were durably inscribed. The redeemer and seeing-God passage at 19:25–27 belongs to this address. This acquisition verifies the KJV wording and its printed alternatives; it does not identify the redeemer by importing a later Christian or Jungian interpretation.

**Job 20:1–21:34 — Zophar again, then Job.** Zophar describes wealth taken through oppression as food that turns to poison and is expelled. Job counters with the prosperity and apparent security of the wicked, the different conditions in which people die, and their common burial. He challenges the friends' explanations as inadequate consolation. The account preserves both speeches rather than treating imagery of consumption as a free-standing ethical doctrine of the whole book.

**Job 22:1–24:25 — Eliphaz's accusations and Job's further protest.** Eliphaz now specifies alleged wrongs against the hungry, naked, widows and fatherless, and urges Job to return to God. Job wants access to the divine judgement-seat and believes a hearing would vindicate him, yet cannot find God in any direction and fears the divine purpose. Chapter 24 widens the complaint to dispossession, exploited labour, the exposed poor, murder and concealed violence. Job's question reaches beyond his own loss.

**Job 25:1–27:23 — the abbreviated final exchange.** Bildad gives a short speech on divine dominion and human impurity. Job asks how such speech helps the powerless, evokes divine action beyond the little heard of it, and maintains his integrity. Chapter 27 also describes the fate of the wicked under Job's continuing speech heading. The selected text does not provide a third Zophar speech or license redistributing these verses into a tidier symmetrical cycle. Such textual-critical reconstruction would require another source task.

**Job 28:1–28 — wisdom, extraction and price.** The poem describes human skill reaching hidden mineral wealth, cutting through rock and bringing darkness to light. It then asks where wisdom can be found. Depth and sea deny possessing it; precious metals and stones cannot purchase it. God knows its way, and the conclusion relates human wisdom to fear of the Lord and departure from evil. The chapter stands between the Job speech headings at 27:1 and 29:1 without introducing a named female actor. Its literary voice and compositional history are not settled by this digital witness.

**Job 29:1–31:40 — remembered standing, humiliation and the final oath.** Job remembers respected public judgement, protection of the vulnerable and intimacy with God. Chapter 30 reverses that standing through contempt, bodily agony, failed hearing and mourning. Chapter 31 develops an oath of integrity concerning desire, deceit, servants, the poor, widow and fatherless, wealth, worship, enemies, hospitality and land. The shared maker of master and servant matters to his answerability. He asks for a hearing and a written charge that he would carry openly. His words end after the land-related oath; the book has not ended with his demand.

**Job 32:1–22 — Elihu enters after the three have ceased.** Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, is angry both at Job's self-justification in relation to God and at the three friends' condemnation without an answer. He explains his previous deference to age and his conviction that understanding comes from divine inspiration rather than age alone. He promises his own answer and rejects flattering partiality. His entrance is a new speech situation, not another name for one of the first three friends.

**Job 33:1–33 — Elihu on address and instruction through affliction.** Elihu speaks as one made of clay and animated by divine breath, inviting a reply without terror. He answers the claims he attributes to Job and presents dreams, pain, a messenger or interpreter, and deliverance as ways God instructs and rescues. The argument is Elihu's account of suffering's possible instructive office; it is not the narrator revealing a hidden cause of Job's losses.

**Job 34:1–35:16 — Elihu on justice and the reach of human action.** Elihu invites judgement upon words, insists that God does no wickedness or partial injustice, and charges Job with speaking without knowledge and adding rebellion. He distinguishes the effect of human righteousness or wickedness upon other people from any profit or injury conferred upon God. He returns to cries of oppression, pride, unanswered prayer and trust. His characterisation of Job must not silently replace Job's own words.

**Job 36:1–37:24 — Elihu's final instruction and weather.** Elihu continues to speak on God's behalf, treating affliction as an opening for discipline while urging Job away from iniquity. Rain, clouds, thunder, snow, frost and winds develop the reach of divine action. He asks Job to consider works he cannot govern or comprehend and closes on divine majesty, justice and human fear. These six chapters must remain between Job's final oath and the LORD's answer.

**Job 38:1–39:30 — the LORD's first speech from the whirlwind.** The LORD answers Job with questions about foundations, the sea's birth and bounds, dawn, death, light, weather, constellations and the provision of food. Rain reaches land with no human inhabitant. The questions pass through lions and ravens, wild goats and deer, the free wild ass, the animal this KJV calls unicorn, ostrich, warhorse, hawk and eagle. Their lives exceed Job's administration. The speech gives no retrospective disclosure to Job of the councils in chapters 1–2.

**Job 40:1–41:34 — Job's first response, the second speech and the creatures.** Asked to answer, Job places his hand over his mouth and declines to proceed. The LORD speaks again from the whirlwind, challenging the relation between Job's righteousness and his condemnation of divine judgement, and asking whether he can humble the proud and save himself. Behemoth is presented as made alongside him and sustained within its habitat. Leviathan resists capture, service, trade, play and weapons; its power and fearlessness culminate the speech. The printed notes conjecturing extinct animals are editorial glosses in this witness, not clauses of the biblical verses and not verified zoological identifications.

**Job 42:1–17 — response, rebuke, intercession and renewed life.** Job acknowledges power and speech beyond his understanding, moves from hearing to seeing, and in this KJV wording abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD then rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for failing to speak rightly as Job has. They must bring seven bullocks and seven rams and receive Job's prayer; they obey, and Job is accepted. Restoration is narrated with his intercession. Kin and acquaintances return, share food, comfort him over the evil the LORD brought upon him, and bring gifts. Livestock numbers double. Seven sons and three daughters are reported; the daughters are named Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch and receive inheritance among their brothers. Job lives another 140 years, sees four generations and dies full of days. The ending does not narrate the first children's resurrection or make renewed prosperity cancel the losses already told. Elihu is not named among the three rebuked friends, and the epilogue does not provide a separate explicit judgement on his speeches.

<a id="biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q001"></a>
### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q001` — Integrity challenged through two councils

This is Satan's question at **Job 1:9**. The surrounding sequence distinguishes a challenge concerning protected prosperity from the later challenge concerning bodily survival. Permission is bounded differently at 1:12 and 2:6. At 2:3 the LORD still affirms Job's integrity and describes the attack as without cause. The wife's challenge at 2:9 and Job's immediate reply belong after that second council.

> Doth Job fear God for nought?

- **Locator:** quotation, Job 1:9, PDF p.2/ii; context, 1:6–2:10, PDF pp.1–5/i–v.
- **Status:** quotation-ready.
- **Verification:** exact sentence checked in the acquired PDF and [same-edition HTML, Job 1](https://ebible.org/eng-kjv2006/JOB01.htm); whole context read. Verification date/verifier and byte identity as above.
- **Source relation:** Extracted sentence; Paraphrased sequence.
- **Use boundary:** preserves the accusation and permissions as narrative events with named speakers. It does not prove that Job's suffering follows a prior moral failure or identify Satan with a later systematic doctrine of evil.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-job` — council, loss and bodily affliction.

<a id="biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q002"></a>
### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q002` — Mourning before explanation

> **Paraphrase:** the three friends arrange to comfort Job, scarcely recognise him, weep, rend their clothing and share seven days and nights of silence. Job then opens his mouth and curses the day of his birth. The friends' subsequent speeches follow his lament; they are not their first response to his loss.

- **Locator:** Job 2:11–3:26, PDF pp.5–7/v–vii.
- **Status:** paraphrase-only.
- **Verification:** read directly across the complete chapter transition in the acquired PDF, 2026-09-08, Codex.
- **Source relation:** Paraphrased.
- **Use boundary:** restores bodily accompaniment and initial silence before doctrinal accusation; distinguishes cursing his day from the curse against God predicted in the councils.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-job` — wife/friends/protest sequence, with wife's prior intervention preserved in q001.

<a id="biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q003"></a>
### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q003` — Protest asks for an answer

> **Paraphrase:** Job asks to reason with God and challenges the friends' dishonest advocacy on God's behalf. He is prepared to speak at personal risk. Later, at the close of his oath, he calls for a hearing and an adversary's written charge, which he would carry openly. Between these moments, complaint, appeal, threatened hope and renewed assertion of integrity develop through the discourses.

- **Locator:** Job 13:3–15, PDF pp.26–27/xxvi–xxvii; 31:35–37, PDF p.63/lxiii. Context: Job 4–27 and 29–31, read entire in their printed speaker order.
- **Status:** paraphrase-only.
- **Verification:** both exact verse spans checked in acquired PDF; context read through every intervening speech, 2026-09-08, Codex.
- **Source relation:** Paraphrased.
- **Use boundary:** provides Job's active demand for accountable address rather than a summary of passive endurance. The KJV reading at 13:15 is an edition-specific witness, not settlement of Hebrew textual or translation disputes.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-job` — protest, advocacy, hearing and judgement.

<a id="biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q004"></a>
### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q004` — Wisdom beyond extraction and purchase

> **Paraphrase:** people can reach hidden ore, redirect water and expose precious things. Wisdom's place and price elude those accomplishments; depth, sea, wealth, destruction and death do not supply possession of it. God knows its way. The chapter concludes with the human relation of reverence and departure from evil to wisdom and understanding.

- **Locator:** Job 28:1–28, PDF pp.54–56/liv–lvi; specific hinges 28:12–15, 20–23 and 28.
- **Status:** paraphrase-only.

### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q005` — Elihu's intervening six chapters

> **Paraphrase:** Elihu speaks after the three friends cease, angry at Job and at their failure to answer him. He distinguishes his youthful voice from inherited seniority, presents suffering as potentially instructive, defends divine justice, and moves through weather and majesty toward the limits of human knowledge. His speech precedes the LORD's answer and is not identical with it.

Their strength resists capture, instrumental use and the assumption that Job can administer the whole order he judges.

<a id="biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q007"></a>
### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q007` — Hearing and seeing before the friends' rebuke

This sentence belongs to Job's response, **42:5**. It is followed by his KJV statement of abhorrence and repentance, then by the LORD's judgement against Eliphaz and his two friends and instruction that Job intercede for them. Job's humbled response and the rebuke of the friends must both survive a retelling.

> I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.

- **Locator:** quotation, Job 42:5, PDF p.87/lxxxvii; context42:1–9, PDF pp.87–88/lxxxvii–lxxxviii.

- **Source relation:** Extracted sentence; Paraphrased sequence.

It does not by itself establish a QL derivation or turn every preceding statement by Job into a doctrinally endorsed proposition. Translation questions at42:6 remain separate from verification of this KJV witness.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-job` — response, rebuke and intercession.

### Passage card — `biblical-job-kjv-ebible-eng-kjv2006-q008` — Restoration with social and familial aftermath

> **Paraphrase:** as Job prays for his friends, his condition is restored. His wider family and former acquaintances return with food, comfort and gifts. Livestock numbers are doubled; seven sons and three named daughters are reported, and the daughters share inheritance among their brothers. He lives another140 years, sees four generations and dies full of days.

- **Locator:** Job 42:10–17, PDF pp.88–89/lxxxviii–lxxxix; comparison1:2–3 and1:18–19, PDF pp.1 and3/i andiii.

- **Verification:** the whole epilogue read against the opening inventory and original losses in the same acquired PDF, 2026-09-08, Codex.
- **Source relation:** Paraphrased.

## Essay uses and source boundaries

The existing admitted `mytheme-job` has its current home at `submission-package/essay/symbolon/mytheme/worlds/biblical/job/WHOLE.md`. This house **sources** its biblical telling; the parent will bind the source into the current page packet and own consumer links. No Job whole is written in this acquisition phase, and no sixfold or symbolic interpretation is ratified by creating this source identity.

[Jung, *Psychology and Religion: West and East*, CW11](../../../psychology/jung/jung-1969-psychology-religion-cw11/jung-1969-psychology-religion-cw11.md) is a separate source house for a psychological interpretation. Its current canonical record was read and has no selected verified excerpts. The acquisition here neither modifies that record nor promotes its quotation status. In particular, **Sophia is not added as a character in this biblical Job witness**. A Jungian Sophia relation must be attributed to Jung and acquired under the selected CW11 edition before quotation; it cannot be smuggled into a biblical narrative by citing chapter28. Biblical characters, speaker assertions, editorial annotations, subsequent reception and Taylor's authored refraction retain distinct provenance.

## Open acquisition and verification

The complete **selected English digital witness is acquired and read**; no chapter is missing. Citation readiness and the two quoted sentences are established for this exact witness. The other six cards are deliberately paraphrase-only. Hebrew philology, date/authorship and composition history, alternative translations at13:15,19:25–27 and42:6, and the species/reception of Behemoth and Leviathan require separate evidence if those claims enter the work. Their absence does not reopen the acquisition of these42 chapters.

Parent tasks: bind the current Job packet; repair declared consumers and reciprocal routes; rebuild/check source projections and run hygiene at the agreed barrier. The present source phase claims none of those operations. The acquisition receipt records admission-before-creation, bytes, complete read coverage and checks.
